Name: orphan_feature_triage
Title: Signal or Artifact? A Prospective, Externally-Grounded Protocol for Triaging Unannotated Discovery Features in Scientific Foundation Models
Short Hypothesis: Sparse-autoencoder features of scientific foundation models that do NOT map onto any existing annotation ('orphan features') fall into two separable classes: (a) genuine latent scientific signals that predict independent, held-out external measurements the model never saw, and (b) technical/dataset artifacts. We hypothesize these two classes are distinguishable in advance by a small set of cheap, model-internal and cross-modal criteria - external-modality predictivity, cross-dataset stability, and causal ablation specificity - yielding a reusable triage protocol that turns interpretability from post-hoc confirmation into prospective, validated discovery.
Related Work: A wave of dictionary-learning work extracts SAE features from scientific FMs and validates them against KNOWN annotations: InterPLM (2024) and Adams et al. (2025) on protein LMs, Discovering Interpretable Biological Concepts in scRNA-seq FMs (2025), SAEs Reveal Interpretable Features in Single-Cell FMs (2025), ICFL on microscopy FMs (2024), and Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with SAEs (2025). All of these note that MANY features do NOT map to existing annotations, and InterPLM/ICFL propose auto-interpretation to label them - but auto-interpretation still hallucinates and cannot distinguish a real undiscovered signal from an artifact. The Pleiades Alzheimer's biomarker study (2026) shows interpretability CAN surface a genuinely novel biomarker class (fragmentomics), but it is a single bespoke success validated by heavy downstream work, not a general triage rule. 'On the definition and importance of interpretability in SciML' (2025) argues that without prior knowledge one cannot tell whether a discovered structure is meaningful. The critical, unaddressed gap is a GENERAL, PROSPECTIVE decision procedure that, for an arbitrary orphan (unannotated) feature, predicts whether it is a real latent signal or an artifact BEFORE expensive follow-up. Our protocol - using cross-modal external ground truth the model never ingested plus cross-dataset stability and causal ablation as a triage classifier - is that missing piece, and is distinct from all prior annotation-matching and single-case discovery work.
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders now routinely extract thousands of interpretable features from scientific foundation models of proteins, cells, and images, and the field has begun to celebrate features that align with known biological concepts. But every such study reports a large fraction of 'orphan' features that map onto no existing annotation, and interpretability's promise for discovery hinges precisely on these: some are undiscovered scientific signals, others are dataset artifacts (batch effects, sequencing depth, staining, plate position), and current practice - auto-interpretation by a stronger LLM - cannot reliably tell them apart. We propose the first general, prospective triage protocol that decides, for an arbitrary unannotated feature, whether it is a genuine latent signal or an artifact, and validates the decision against independent evidence the model never saw. Working with public single-cell RNA-seq foundation models (scGPT, Geneformer) and protein language models (ESM-2), we train SAEs, remove features matching known annotations, and score the remaining orphans on three cheap criteria: (1) external-modality predictivity - does the feature predict a held-out measurement from a DIFFERENT modality/assay the model was never trained on (e.g., a scRNA feature predicting matched CITE-seq surface-protein levels, or an ESM-2 feature predicting an experimental deep-mutational-scanning quantity)? (2) cross-dataset stability - does an equivalent feature reappear across independent datasets/labs? (3) causal ablation specificity - does ablating it selectively change model outputs for a coherent biological subset, not diffusely? We test whether these three criteria jointly separate a curated set of known-signal orphans from planted-artifact orphans, calibrate a triage classifier, and then apply it prospectively to surface and externally confirm candidate novel signals. The result is a reusable instrument that converts interpretability from confirmation into validated discovery. The contribution is a decision protocol, not a new SAE method: its novelty is the prospective triage rule and the cross-modal external ground truth it is validated against, distinct from prior annotation-recovery and LLM auto-labeling that can only confirm known concepts or hallucinate labels. The user story is concrete, an interpretability practitioner runs it on their own SAE features, on any scientific FM, before committing wet-lab or downstream-enrichment follow-up, and the payoff is quantified as discovery precision at K over a random-orphan baseline and the cost of chasing artifacts avoided. If it only partially works, the calibrated classifier is still usable as a ranked prioritizer with reported precision and recall rather than a hard filter, and the three-criterion design is intended to transfer beyond the showcased modalities.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- feature extraction, orphan set, and a two-class development set of known-signal vs planted-artifact orphans): Establishes the substrate and the ground-truth labels that clauses (a)/(b) and the triage claim are tested on -- namely that orphan SAE features split into genuine latent scientific signals and technical/dataset artifacts. Data: two scRNA-seq FMs (scGPT ~51M and Geneformer ~10-40M or scFoundation) and a protein LM (ESM-2 650M), public weights, frozen (inference-only); SAEs are the only trainable objects. We train TopK SAEs (dictionary width 16x hidden dim, k=32, Adam lr 1e-4, up to ~1e8 token-activations, 3 SAE seeds) on one hidden layer of each model, following InterPLM/single-cell SAE recipes. Each feature is matched to known annotations (cell type, tissue, cell-cycle phase, GO terms, secondary structure, binding sites) by activation-vs-label alignment; features with F1 or AUROC >= 0.7 are 'annotated', the remainder are ORPHANS. From the orphans we build a labeled development set: KNOWN-SIGNAL orphans = features correlating (Spearman >= 0.5) with an independently-validated signature deliberately held out of the annotation set; PLANTED-ARTIFACT orphans = features aligning (AUROC >= 0.8) with technical covariates (sequencing depth, batch/lab ID, plate/well position, staining intensity, mitochondrial fraction). Target >= 100 orphans per class per model. Decisive metric first: development-set class balance and label-confidence (fraction with covariate/signature alignment above threshold). Convincing: >= 100 orphans per class per model with confident labels. If fewer than ~40 per class are recoverable for a given model, that model is reported as underpowered and excluded from the decisive triage test rather than analyzed at low power. A negative finding here (orphans do not resolve into the two labeled classes at all) would itself contradict the premise that the classes exist and are identifiable.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Criterion 1, external-modality predictivity separates the two classes): Tests whether external-modality predictivity distinguishes genuine-signal from artifact orphans. Data: the development-set orphans from Experiment 1 (reused). scRNA case: paired CITE-seq (matched cells with ~130-200 surface-protein readouts) and multiome ATAC (existing public sets used as is); protein case: an experimental deep-mutational-scanning fitness set and a mega-scale stability ddG set (existing, used as is). Model: frozen FMs and fixed SAE features; only a ridge/logistic read-out from a feature's activation to the held-out external measurement is fitted (5 seeds, cell/protein-grouped splits). Systems compared: each orphan's cross-modal predictive R^2/AUROC residualized against the matched ANNOTATED features, known-signal vs planted-artifact. Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-1 score for separating known-signal from planted-artifact orphans. Convincing: separation AUROC >= 0.75 with 95% bootstrap CI (over features) excluding 0.5. Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (stated before the data): Criterion 1 is a weak-but-usable signal, retained only as one of three inputs, not a sole arbiter. A negative result means external-modality predictivity does not separate the classes, weakening the triage protocol.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- Criterion 2, cross-dataset stability separates the two classes): Tests whether cross-dataset stability distinguishes the classes. Data: independent datasets from different labs/protocols for each modality (existing public sets); we train independent SAEs (same recipe) on each and match features across dictionaries by activation-correlation and matched top-activating examples. Model: frozen FMs; SAEs trainable. Systems compared: cross-dataset stability score of known-signal vs planted-artifact orphans (genuine signals expected stable; artifacts dataset-specific, or, if stable, covariate-aligned and caught by Criterion 3). Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-2 score for class separation. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 (bootstrap CI over features excluding 0.5). Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (declared up front): weak-but-usable, kept as one of three inputs. We report robustness to SAE width/k because feature splitting/merging can blur matching. A negative result means stability does not separate the classes, weakening the protocol.

Experiment 4 (H1 -- Criterion 3, causal ablation specificity separates the two classes): Tests whether ablation specificity distinguishes the classes. Data: development-set orphans (reused). Model: frozen FMs; we ablate each orphan feature in the SAE reconstruction and measure the induced change in downstream outputs, bounding edits and comparing to matched random-feature ablations. Systems compared: specificity index = concentration of the ablation effect on a coherent biological subset (cell type / protein family) vs diffuse or technical-covariate-aligned change, known-signal vs planted-artifact. Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-3 score for class separation. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 (bootstrap CI over features excluding 0.5). Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (declared before the data): weak-but-usable, one of three inputs. A negative result means ablation specificity does not separate the classes, weakening the protocol.

Experiment 5 (H1 -- triage classifier calibrates and beats the LLM auto-interpretation default): Tests the core claim that the three cheap criteria JOINTLY yield a reusable triage instrument, and that it beats the current default. Data: development-set orphans with the three criterion scores (reused). Model: a logistic-regression triage classifier on the three scores (the only fitted model), with leave-one-model-family-out and leave-one-modality-out cross-validation to test generality; per-criterion ablations to see which carries the signal. Baseline system: LLM auto-interpretation (labeling top-activating examples) confidence used as a predictor of genuine-vs-artifact status. Decisive metric first: cross-validated AUROC of the triage classifier separating known-signal from planted-artifact orphans. Convincing: triage AUROC >= 0.8 that generalizes across held-out model families/modalities (drop <= 0.1) AND exceeds the LLM-auto-interpretation baseline AUROC by >= 0.15. Refute: triage AUROC <= 0.6 or no improvement over the LLM baseline. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.8 (declared up front): a partial instrument -- reported with its precision/recall and error analysis, not advanced as a validated triage rule. A negative result means the cheap criteria do not jointly separate the classes better than the current default, contradicting the central hypothesis.

Experiment 6 (H2 -- prospective, externally-confirmed discovery): Tests the claim that the calibrated triage turns interpretability into prospective, validated discovery -- that top-ranked unlabeled orphans confirm against external evidence not used in triage. Data: the remaining UNLABELED orphans (held out of Experiments 2-5); external confirmation sources not used in triage -- a newer/independent database for enrichment, a matched-cell external assay, and a held-out DMS set. Model: the frozen triage classifier from Experiment 5 applied to unlabeled orphans; no further fitting. Systems compared: confirmation rate of the top-ranked predicted 'genuine signals' vs a random-orphan baseline. Decisive metric first: discovery precision = fraction of top-K predicted-genuine orphans that externally confirm, relative to the random-orphan baseline rate. Convincing: top-K confirmation rate >= 2x the random-orphan baseline with a 95% CI excluding parity, plus 2-3 externally-confirmed novel-signal case studies. Refute: confirmation rate within noise of the random baseline. Indeterminate band: 1.2x-2x baseline (declared before the data) -- suggestive prospective value that does not yet establish the triage as a discovery instrument; reported as such. A negative result means the triage does not prospectively surface genuine signals, contradicting the discovery claim. All work is inference-only on public FMs plus academic-scale SAE training and public paired datasets, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'known-signal vs planted-artifact' development labels may be imperfect; some presumed artifacts could carry biology and vice versa. We mitigate by using clearly technical covariates (depth, batch, plate) for artifacts and independently-validated signatures for signals, and report sensitivity to label noise.

Paired cross-modal data (CITE-seq/multi-omic matched cells, DMS with sequence) is limited in quantity and coverage, which constrains Criterion 1; we use the best available public paired datasets and treat cross-modal predictivity as one of three criteria rather than the sole arbiter.

Some genuine signals may be dataset-specific (cross-dataset stability fails) and some artifacts may be stable across labs; the three criteria are designed to be complementary so no single failure is decisive, but the triage classifier may still misclassify edge cases - we report calibration and error analysis rather than claim perfect separation.

SAE features can be split/merged across dictionaries, complicating cross-dataset matching; we use matched-top-example and activation-correlation matching and report robustness to SAE hyperparameters and width.
Ablation in SAE reconstruction may push activations off-manifold; we bound edits and report specificity relative to matched random-feature ablations.

External confirmation of prospectively-surfaced novel signals is inherently harder to guarantee within one paper; we frame the contribution primarily as a validated TRIAGE INSTRUMENT (evaluated on the development set with ground truth) plus a small number of externally-confirmed case studies, so the paper stands even if only a few novel signals confirm.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus academic-scale SAE training and public paired datasets, keeping compute feasible for an academic lab.
